claim: LGC-46 is a member of the Cys-loop acetylcholine (ACh)-gated chloride (ACC) channel family.
source: Here we report that C. elegans LGC-46, a member of the Cys-loop acetylcholine (ACh)-gated chloride (ACC) channel family, localizes to presynaptic terminals of cholinergic motor neurons and regulates synaptic vesicle (SV) release kinetics upon evoked release of acetylcholine.
evidence: The manuscript states this directly in the abstract and provides phylogenetic analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B showing LGC-46 clustering with ACC family members.

claim: LGC-46 localizes to presynaptic terminals of cholinergic motor neurons.
source: Here we report that C. elegans LGC-46, a member of the Cys-loop acetylcholine (ACh)-gated chloride (ACC) channel family, localizes to presynaptic terminals of cholinergic motor neurons and regulates synaptic vesicle (SV) release kinetics upon evoked release of acetylcholine.
evidence: Directly stated in abstract and demonstrated through imaging data in Figure 1B-F showing LGC-46::GFP punctate localization in dorsal nerve cord and colocalization with presynaptic markers UNC-10 and RAB-3.

claim: Loss of lgc-46 prolongs evoked release without altering spontaneous activity.
source: Loss of lgc-46 prolongs evoked release, without altering spontaneous activity.
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 2 showing prolonged decay phase of eEPSCs in lgc-46(0) mutants while endogenous EPSC frequency and amplitude remain normal.

claim: A gain-of-function mutation of lgc-46 shortens evoked release to reduce synaptic transmission.
source: Conversely, a gain-of-function mutation of lgc-46 shortens evoked release to reduce synaptic transmission.
evidence: Stated in abstract and demonstrated by electrophysiology data in Figure 4 showing reduced amplitude and shortened decay phase of eEPSCs in lgc-46(gf) mutants.

claim: The inhibition of presynaptic release by LGC-46 requires the anion selectivity of the channel.
source: This inhibition of presynaptic release requires the anion selectivity of LGC-46, and can ameliorate cholinergic over-excitation in a C. elegans model of excitation-inhibition imbalance.
evidence: Stated in abstract and demonstrated in Figure 3C showing that PAR motif mutant LGC-46(M314I) does not suppress acr-2(gf) convulsions, while wild-type PAR motif LGC-46(M314I) does.

claim: LGC-46 can ameliorate cholinergic over-excitation in a C. elegans model of excitation-inhibition imbalance.
source: This inhibition of presynaptic release requires the anion selectivity of LGC-46, and can ameliorate cholinergic over-excitation in a C. elegans model of excitation-inhibition imbalance.
evidence: Stated in abstract and demonstrated in Figure 3A showing lgc-46(ju825) suppresses acr-2(gf) convulsions.

claim: Cys-loop LGICs participate in rapid regulation of neurotransmission by changing plasma membrane conductance upon ligand binding.
source: Cys-loop Ligand-gated ion channels (LGICs) participate in rapid regulation of neurotransmission by changing the plasma membrane conductance upon ligand binding (Keramidas et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a general statement about LGIC function supported by a citation to Keramidas et al., 2004.

claim: Classical electrophysiological recordings from cat spinal cord showed that activation of flexor afferent neurons caused decreased excitatory transmission of extensor afferent neurons onto extensor motor neurons.
source: For example, classical electrophysiological recordings from cat spinal cord showed that activation of flexor afferent neurons caused decreased excitatory transmission of extensor afferent neurons onto extensor motor neurons (Eccles et al., 1961, 1963; Frank and Fuortes, 1957).
evidence: This historical finding is supported by citations to Eccles et al., 1961, 1963 and Frank and Fuortes, 1957.

claim: The effect of flexor afferent neuron activation on extensor afferent transmission was blocked by picrotoxin.
source: This effect was blocked by picrotoxin, an antagonist of ionotropic GABA receptors, implying that GABAA receptors may be involved in inhibition of presynaptic release (Eccles et al., 1963).
evidence: This finding is supported by citation to Eccles et al., 1963.

claim: Picrotoxin is an antagonist of ionotropic GABA receptors.
source: This effect was blocked by picrotoxin, an antagonist of ionotropic GABA receptors, implying that GABAA receptors may be involved in inhibition of presynaptic release (Eccles et al., 1963).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the context of describing historical experiments.

claim: Extensor afferent neuron terminals receive axo-axonal connections from GABAergic interneurons that are activated by flexor afferent neurons.
source: Ultrastructural studies later revealed that the extensor afferent neuron terminals receive axo-axonal connections from GABAergic interneurons that are activated by flexor afferent neurons (Pierce and Mendell, 1993; Destombes et al., 1996), suggesting the presence of GABA-gated LGICs in presynaptic axons.
evidence: This finding is supported by citations to Pierce and Mendell, 1993 and Destombes et al., 1996.

claim: Stimulation of inhibitory motor neurons in crayfish opener muscles caused decreased neurotransmission from excitatory motor neurons.
source: It was shown that stimulation of inhibitory motor neurons caused decreased neurotransmission from excitatory motor neurons, and that statistical analysis of excitatory transmitter quanta suggested a likely presynaptic effect (Dudel and Kuffler, 1961).
evidence: This finding is supported by citation to Dudel and Kuffler, 1961.

claim: Addition of exogenous GABA at crayfish neuromuscular junctions caused effects similar to inhibitory motor neuron stimulation, which was relieved by picrotoxin.
source: Addition of exogenous GABA at these neuromuscular junctions caused similar effects, which was relieved by picrotoxin (Takeuchi and Takeuchi, 1966, 1969), suggesting this presynaptic inhibition involves GABA-gated LGICs in the presynaptic axons.
evidence: This finding is supported by citations to Takeuchi and Takeuchi, 1966, 1969.

claim: Several ionotropic glycine receptors and GABAA receptors act in presynaptic cells to regulate synaptic transmission in the mammalian central nervous system.
source: Studies in the past decades have subsequently identified several ionotropic glycine receptors and GABAA receptors acting in the presynaptic cells to regulate synaptic transmission in the mammalian central nervous system (Kullmann et al., 2005; Engelman and MacDermott, 2004).
evidence: This finding is supported by citations to Kullmann et al., 2005 and Engelman and MacDermott, 2004.

claim: Acetylcholine provides major excitatory inputs to the body wall muscles in the C. elegans locomotor circuit.
source: In C. elegans locomotor circuit, acetylcholine provides major excitatory inputs to the body wall muscles (Richmond and Jorgensen, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Richmond and Jorgensen, 1999.

claim: C. elegans genome encodes a large number of LGICs, many of which are known or predicted to be responsive to acetylcholine.
source: C. elegans genome encodes a large number of LGICs, many of which are known or predicted to be responsive to acetylcholine (Hobert, 2013; Jones and Sattelle, 2008), but whether they regulate SV release at presynaptic terminals is not known.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hobert, 2013 and Jones and Sattelle, 2008.

claim: lgc-46 is strongly expressed in cholinergic motor neurons and weakly expressed in GABAergic motor neurons.
source: Co-expression of Plgc-46-GFP with markers for cholinergic (Punc-17-mCherry) and GABAergic (Pttr-39-mCherry) neurons revealed that lgc-46 was strongly expressed in cholinergic motor neurons, and weakly expressed in GABAergic motor neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by colocalization experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: LGC-46::GFP was detected only in the dorsal nerve cords in L1 stage animals.
source: In the first larval (L1) stage animals, cholinergic motor neurons form synapses onto dorsal body wall muscles (Sulston, 1976; White et al., 1978), and we observed LGC-46::GFP only in the dorsal nerve cords (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly observed and shown in Figure 1B, with supporting citations about cholinergic motor neuron anatomy.

claim: LGC-46::GFP expressed in DA9 neuron was detected only in the dorsal side of L4 and adult animals.
source: We also expressed LGC-46::GFP in a single cholinergic motor neuron DA9, which synapses onto dorsal body wall muscles, and found LGC-46::GFP was detected only in the dorsal side of L4 and adult animals (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is directly observed and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: LGC-46 primarily localizes to the axonal compartment of cholinergic motor neurons.
source: These results indicate that LGC-46 primarily localizes to the axonal compartment of cholinergic motor neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that LGC-46::GFP is only detected in dorsal nerve cords where cholinergic motor neurons form synapses.

claim: LGC-46::GFP displayed a high degree of overlap with UNC-10.
source: To determine if the punctate pattern of LGC-46::GFP corresponded to presynaptic terminals, we co-immunostained LGC-46::GFP together with endogenous active zone protein RIM/UNC-10 (Figure 1D). LGC-46::GFP displayed a high degree of overlap with UNC-10.
evidence: This is demonstrated by colocalization imaging in Figure 1D and quantified in Figure 1F.

claim: LGC-46::GFP showed co-localization with synaptic vesicle marker mCherry::RAB-3 expressed in cholinergic motor neurons.
source: Additionally, we found that LGC-46::GFP showed co-localization with a synaptic vesicle marker mCherry::RAB-3 expressed in cholinergic motor neurons (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by colocalization imaging in Figure 1E and quantified in Figure 1F.

claim: LGC-46 is the first reported LGIC localized to presynaptic terminals in C. elegans.
source: To our knowledge LGC-46 is the first reported LGIC localized to presynaptic terminals in C. elegans.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Cholinergic synapse morphology and density in lgc-46(0) mutants were comparable to those in wild type.
source: Cholinergic synapse morphology and density in lgc-46(0) mutants were comparable to those in wild type (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B), and lgc-46(0) animals displayed normal growth, reproduction and locomotion.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: lgc-46(0) animals displayed normal growth, reproduction and locomotion.
source: Cholinergic synapse morphology and density in lgc-46(0) mutants were comparable to those in wild type (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B), and lgc-46(0) animals displayed normal growth, reproduction and locomotion.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the authors' experiments.

claim: lgc-46(0) animals were hypersensitive to aldicarb.
source: lgc-46(0) animals were hypersensitive to aldicarb, an inhibitor of acetylcholine esterase, while they showed normal sensitivity to levamisole, an agonist for the postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors on muscles (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pharmacological assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: lgc-46(0) animals showed normal sensitivity to levamisole.
source: lgc-46(0) animals were hypersensitive to aldicarb, an inhibitor of acetylcholine esterase, while they showed normal sensitivity to levamisole, an agonist for the postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors on muscles (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pharmacological assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Aldicarb is an inhibitor of acetylcholine esterase.
source: lgc-46(0) animals were hypersensitive to aldicarb, an inhibitor of acetylcholine esterase, while they showed normal sensitivity to levamisole, an agonist for the postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors on muscles (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the drug.

claim: Levamisole is an agonist for the postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors on muscles.
source: lgc-46(0) animals were hypersensitive to aldicarb, an inhibitor of acetylcholine esterase, while they showed normal sensitivity to levamisole, an agonist for the postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors on muscles (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the drug.

claim: The hypersensitivity to aldicarb in lgc-46(0) was rescued by specific expression of LGC-46 in cholinergic motor neurons.
source: The hypersensitivity to aldicarb was rescued by specific expression of LGC-46 in cholinergic motor neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that LGC-46 likely represses cholinergic motor neuron activities.
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The amplitude of eEPSCs in lgc-46(0) animals was comparable to that in wild type.
source: We found that the amplitude of eEPSCs in lgc-46(0) animals was comparable to that in wild type (Figure 2A,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2A and 2C.

claim: The rise phase of eEPSCs in lgc-46(0) was similar to wild type.
source: The rise phase of eEPSCs was similar to wild type, suggesting the onset of evoked cholinergic transmission is not affected (Figure 2B,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2B and 2D.

claim: eEPSCs in lgc-46(0) were prolonged and displayed a significantly slower decay than that of wild type.
source: However, the analysis of release kinetics revealed that eEPSCs in lgc-46(0) were prolonged and displayed a significantly slower decay than that of wild type.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2A, 2B, and 2D.

claim: lgc-46(0) mutants displayed a normal early phase of SV release (21.33 ± 2.50 pC, compared to 18.41 ± 1.68 pC in wild type).
source: Specifically, lgc-46(0) mutants displayed a normal early phase of SV release (21.33 ± 2.50 pC, compared to 18.41 ± 1.68 pC in wild type), but exhibited a large increase in the late phase (18.06 ± 2.19 pC, compared to 11.35 ± 1.35 pC in wild type).
evidence: This is quantified from cumulative charge transfer analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: lgc-46(0) mutants exhibited a large increase in the late phase of SV release (18.06 ± 2.19 pC, compared to 11.35 ± 1.35 pC in wild type).
source: Specifically, lgc-46(0) mutants displayed a normal early phase of SV release (21.33 ± 2.50 pC, compared to 18.41 ± 1.68 pC in wild type), but exhibited a large increase in the late phase (18.06 ± 2.19 pC, compared to 11.35 ± 1.35 pC in wild type).
evidence: This is quantified from cumulative charge transfer analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Both the slow decay of eEPSCs and the increased late phase of SV release in lgc-46(0) were rescued by expression of LGC-46 in cholinergic motor neurons.
source: Both the slow decay of eEPSCs and the increased late phase of SV release were rescued by expression of LGC-46 in cholinergic motor neurons (Figure 2A–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments shown in Figure 2A-E.

claim: The frequency of endogenous EPSCs in lgc-46(0) mutants was comparable to that in wild type.
source: The frequency of endogenous EPSCs in lgc-46(0) mutants was comparable to that in wild type (Figure 2F), indicating that cholinergic transmission in the resting condition was not affected.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The amplitude and kinetics of endogenous EPSCs were normal in lgc-46(0) mutants.
source: The amplitude and kinetics of endogenous EPSCs were normal in lgc-46(0) mutants (Figure 2F; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D), confirming that the slow decay of evoked release was not due to altered kinetics of postsynaptic receptor response on muscles.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: LGC-46 acts as an auto-receptor to inhibit presynaptic activities upon synaptic vesicle release.
source: As LGC-46 resides in the presynaptic terminals of cholinergic motor neurons, these data support a conclusion that LGC-46 acts as an auto-receptor to inhibit presynaptic activities upon synaptic vesicle release.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the combination of localization data and functional data showing LGC-46 affects evoked but not spontaneous release.

claim: Cholinergic motor neurons express the ACR-2 ACh-gated cation channel in their dendrites and soma.
source: Cholinergic motor neurons express the ACR-2 ACh-gated cation channel in their dendrites and soma (Jospin et al., 2009; Qi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jospin et al., 2009 and Qi et al., 2013.

claim: acr-2(gf) mutation contains a missense mutation in the transmembrane domain 2, similar to those found in CHNR2B of human epilepsy patients.
source: We previously characterized an acr-2(gf) mutation that contains a missense mutation in the transmembrane domain 2, similar to those found in CHNR2B of human epilepsy patients (Phillips et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Phillips et al., 2001 for the human epilepsy connection.

claim: ACR-2(gf) increases channel activity and causes hyperactivity of cholinergic motor neurons.
source: ACR-2(gf) increases channel activity and causes hyperactivity of cholinergic motor neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a previously characterized finding.

claim: acr-2(gf) animals show distinctive spontaneous convulsions due to an altered ratio of excitation and inhibition in the locomotor circuit.
source: acr-2(gf) animals show distinctive spontaneous convulsions, due to an altered ratio of excitation and inhibition in the locomotor circuit (Jospin et al., 2009; Qi et al., 2013; Stawicki et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jospin et al., 2009; Qi et al., 2013; and Stawicki et al., 2013.

claim: lgc-46(ju825) mutation strongly suppressed the convulsion of acr-2(gf).
source: By screening for suppressors of the acr-2(gf) convulsion behavior (see Materials and methods), we isolated a lgc-46(ju825) mutation that strongly suppressed the convulsion of acr-2(gf) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The lgc-46(ju825) mutation causes a substitution of methionine to isoleucine (M314I) in the pore-lining transmembrane TM2 domain.
source: We determined that the lgc-46(ju825) mutation causes a substitution of methionine to isoleucine (M314I) in the pore-lining transmembrane TM2 domain (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is determined by sequencing and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: lgc-46(0) did not show significant effects on acr-2(gf) convulsion.
source: lgc-46(0) did not show significant effects on acr-2(gf) convulsion (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Transgenic overexpression of LGC-46(M314I), but not LGC-46(WT), driven by lgc-46 promoter strongly suppressed acr-2(gf) convulsion.
source: In addition, transgenic overexpression of LGC-46(M314I), but not LGC-46(WT), driven by lgc-46 promoter strongly suppressed acr-2(gf) convulsion.
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: lgc-46(ju825) is a gain-of-function mutation.
source: These data indicate that lgc-46(ju825) is a gain-of-function mutation, designated as lgc-46(gf) hereafter.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that lgc-46(ju825) suppresses acr-2(gf) while lgc-46(0) does not, and overexpression of LGC-46(M314I) mimics the suppression.

claim: Pan-neuronal and cholinergic LGC-46(M314I) expression suppressed acr-2(gf) convulsions.
source: By expressing lgc-46 in a cell-type specific manner, we found that pan-neuronal and cholinergic LGC-46(M314I) expression suppressed acr-2(gf) convulsions whereas its expression in muscles or GABAergic motor neurons had no effect (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell-type specific rescue experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: LGC-46(M314I) expression in muscles or GABAergic motor neurons had no effect on acr-2(gf) convulsions.
source: By expressing lgc-46 in a cell-type specific manner, we found that pan-neuronal and cholinergic LGC-46(M314I) expression suppressed acr-2(gf) convulsions whereas its expression in muscles or GABAergic motor neurons had no effect (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell-type specific rescue experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: acr-2(gf) shows hypersensitivity to both aldicarb and levamisole.
source: acr-2(gf) shows hypersensitivity to both aldicarb and levamisole (Jospin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jospin et al., 2009.

claim: lgc-46(ju825) partially suppressed the aldicarb hypersensitivity, but not the levamisole sensitivity of acr-2(gf).
source: lgc-46(ju825) partially suppressed the aldicarb hypersensitivity, but not the levamisole sensitivity of acr-2(gf) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D), suggesting that lgc-46(ju825) likely affects presynaptic activity of cholinergic neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by pharmacological assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: Expression of LGC-46(M314I) in cholinergic motor neurons fully suppressed the aldicarb hypersensitivity of lgc-46(0).
source: Consistently, expression of LGC-46(M314I) in cholinergic motor neurons also fully suppressed the aldicarb hypersensitivity of lgc-46(0) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: lgc-46 acts cell-autonomously to suppress cholinergic neuron activities.
source: These data show that lgc-46 acts cell-autonomously to suppress cholinergic neuron activities.
evidence: This is inferred from cell-type specific rescue experiments showing that expression in cholinergic neurons is sufficient for suppression.

claim: The presence of the PAR motif preceding TM2 is crucial for ion selectivity in LGC-46.
source: LGC-46 is predicted to be an anion-conducting channel, and the presence of the PAR motif preceding TM2 is crucial for ion selectivity (Galzi et al., 1992; Keramidas et al., 2000; Jensen et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Galzi et al., 1992; Keramidas et al., 2000; and Jensen et al., 2005.

claim: PAR-mutant LGC-46(M314I) did not suppress acr-2(gf) convulsions when expressed in cholinergic motor neurons.
source: When expressed in cholinergic motor neurons, PAR-mutant LGC-46(M314I) did not suppress acr-2(gf) convulsions (Figure 3C), consistent with LGC-46 acting as an anion-selective channel.
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral assays shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The M314I mutation does not alter LGC-46 localization.
source: The M314I mutation does not alter LGC-46 localization as functional GFP-tagged LGC-46(M314I) showed restricted expression at presynaptic terminals, similar to wild type ().
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: lgc-46(gf) mutants showed significantly reduced amplitudes of eEPSCs compared to wild type.
source: lgc-46(gf) mutants showed significantly reduced amplitudes of eEPSCs and release kinetics with much shorter decay phase compared to wild type, whereas the time constant of the rise phase of eEPSCs was not affected (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: lgc-46(gf) mutants showed release kinetics with much shorter decay phase compared to wild type.
source: lgc-46(gf) mutants showed significantly reduced amplitudes of eEPSCs and release kinetics with much shorter decay phase compared to wild type, whereas the time constant of the rise phase of eEPSCs was not affected (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: The time constant of the rise phase of eEPSCs was not affected in lgc-46(gf) mutants.
source: lgc-46(gf) mutants showed significantly reduced amplitudes of eEPSCs and release kinetics with much shorter decay phase compared to wild type, whereas the time constant of the rise phase of eEPSCs was not affected (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: The charge transfer during eEPSCs was significantly reduced in lgc-46(gf) mutants.
source: Consequently, the charge transfer during eEPSCs was significantly reduced in lgc-46(gf) mutants, indicating the inhibition of SV release (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cumulative charge transfer analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The amplitude and kinetics of endogenous EPSCs were not affected in lgc-46(gf) mutants.
source: We also recorded endogenous release and found that, similar to lgc-46(0), the amplitude and kinetics of endogenous EPSCs were not affected in lgc-46(gf) mutants (Figure 4F; Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G-H.

claim: lgc-46(gf) significantly reduced the frequency of endogenous EPSCs.
source: However, lgc-46(gf) significantly reduced the frequency of endogenous EPSCs, suggesting the lower excitability in cholinergic motor neurons compared to wild type (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Expression of LGC-46(M314I) in lgc-46(0) mutant background mimicked the characteristics of reduced amplitude and shortened decay of evoked release from the lgc-46(gf) animals.
source: Expression of LGC-46(M314I) in lgc-46(0) mutant background mimicked the characteristics of reduced amplitude and shortened decay of evoked release from the lgc-46(gf) animals (Figure 4A–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments shown in Figure 4A-F.

claim: LGC-46(M314I) can function as an overactive anion channel, thereby suppressing SV release more efficiently than wild type LGC-46.
source: These results suggest that LGC-46(M314I) can function as an overactive anion channel, thereby suppressing SV release more efficiently than wild type LGC-46.
evidence: This is inferred from the gain-of-function phenotypes showing enhanced inhibition of synaptic release.

claim: Some ACC family proteins can form homomeric or heteromeric channels which respond to acetylcholine when expressed in Xenopus oocytes.
source: Some ACC family proteins can form homomeric or heteromeric channels, which respond to acetylcholine when expressed in Xenopus oocytes (Putrenko et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Putrenko et al., 2005.

claim: Studies of LGC-46 have not yet revealed ACh-gated channel activity.
source: Similar studies of LGC-46 have not yet revealed ACh-gated channel activity (Joseph Dent, personal communication), or responsiveness to other neurotransmitters (Ringstad et al., 2009), suggesting that LGC-46 may require additional subunits or accessory factors to form a functional channel.
evidence: This is stated based on personal communication and citation to Ringstad et al., 2009.

claim: LGC-46 may require additional subunits or accessory factors to form a functional channel.
source: Similar studies of LGC-46 have not yet revealed ACh-gated channel activity (Joseph Dent, personal communication), or responsiveness to other neurotransmitters (Ringstad et al., 2009), suggesting that LGC-46 may require additional subunits or accessory factors to form a functional channel.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of observed channel activity in heterologous expression systems.

claim: lgc-46(gf) animals display a curly body posture and slow locomotion.
source: To identify potential interacting partners, we took advantage of a behavioral phenotype of lgc-46(gf). These animals display a curly body posture and slow locomotion (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by locomotion assays shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Expression of LGC-46(M314I) under its own promoter in lgc-46(0) background mimicked the locomotion phenotypes.
source: Expression of LGC-46(M314I) under its own promoter in lgc-46(0) background mimicked the locomotion phenotypes, indicating that LGC-46(M314I) is responsible for the phenotype.
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments showing that the mutant protein is sufficient to cause the phenotype.

claim: All single mutants of acc-1 to acc-4 and lgc-47 to lgc-49 showed grossly normal movement.
source: We systematically examined null mutations in seven other ACC genes (acc-1 to acc-4 and lgc-47 to lgc-49) and observed that all single mutants showed grossly normal movement.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from systematic genetic analysis.

claim: acc-4(0) showed a specific suppression of the lgc-46(gf) phenotype such that double mutant animals regained normal locomotion.
source: We then made double mutants with lgc-46(gf), and found that acc-4(0) showed a specific suppression of the lgc-46(gf) phenotype such that double mutant animals regained normal locomotion (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by locomotion assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: acc-4 was required for the suppression of acr-2(gf) convulsion by lgc-46(gf).
source: acc-4 was also required for the suppression of acr-2(gf) convulsion by lgc-46(gf) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral assays shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ACC-4 is expressed in all cholinergic motor neurons.
source: ACC-4 is expressed in all cholinergic motor neurons (Pereira et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pereira et al., 2015.

claim: Transgenic expression of acc-4, driven by its own promoter, or of an acc-4 cDNA in cholinergic motor neurons rescued the effects of acc-4(0) in lgc-46(gf) acc-4(0); acr-2(gf) background.
source: Transgenic expression of acc-4, driven by its own promoter, or of an acc-4 cDNA in cholinergic motor neurons rescued the effects of acc-4(0) in lgc-46(gf) acc-4(0); acr-2(gf) background (Figure 5A), indicating that both ACC-4 and LGC-46 function in the cholinergic motor neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Both ACC-4 and LGC-46 function in the cholinergic motor neurons.
source: Transgenic expression of acc-4, driven by its own promoter, or of an acc-4 cDNA in cholinergic motor neurons rescued the effects of acc-4(0) in lgc-46(gf) acc-4(0); acr-2(gf) background (Figure 5A), indicating that both ACC-4 and LGC-46 function in the cholinergic motor neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from cell-type specific rescue experiments.

claim: ACC-4::GFP showed axonal punctate localization at presynaptic terminals, similar to LGC-46::GFP.
source: ACC-4::GFP showed axonal punctate localization at presynaptic terminals (Figure 5B–D), similar to LGC-46::GFP.
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figure 5B-D.

claim: acc-4(0) did not affect the punctate localization of LGC-46.
source: acc-4(0) did not affect the punctate localization of LGC-46 (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: ACC-4 and LGC-46 are independently trafficked to the presynaptic site.
source: These results suggest that ACC-4 and LGC-46 are independently trafficked to the presynaptic site.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that loss of acc-4 does not affect LGC-46 localization.

claim: acc-4(0) single mutants showed normal amplitudes of eEPSCs.
source: acc-4(0) single mutants showed normal amplitudes of eEPSCs, but significantly increased eEPSC amplitudes in lgc-46(gf) background (Figure 5F–H), indicating that loss of ACC-4 abolished the gain-of-function effects of LGC-46(M314I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5F-H.

claim: acc-4(0) significantly increased eEPSC amplitudes in lgc-46(gf) background.
source: acc-4(0) single mutants showed normal amplitudes of eEPSCs, but significantly increased eEPSC amplitudes in lgc-46(gf) background (Figure 5F–H), indicating that loss of ACC-4 abolished the gain-of-function effects of LGC-46(M314I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5F-H.

claim: Loss of ACC-4 abolished the gain-of-function effects of LGC-46(M314I).
source: acc-4(0) single mutants showed normal amplitudes of eEPSCs, but significantly increased eEPSC amplitudes in lgc-46(gf) background (Figure 5F–H), indicating that loss of ACC-4 abolished the gain-of-function effects of LGC-46(M314I).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that acc-4(0) reverses the reduced eEPSC amplitude phenotype of lgc-46(gf).

claim: The time constants of the rise phase were not affected in acc-4(0).
source: The time constants of the rise phase were not affected in acc-4(0) (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: acc-4(0) prolonged the decay phase in wild type or in lgc-46(gf) background, similar to lgc-46(0).
source: However, acc-4(0) prolonged the decay phase in wild type or in lgc-46(gf) background, similar to lgc-46(0) (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: LGC-46 and ACC-4 function together in cholinergic motor neurons to regulate the SV release kinetics following neuronal activation.
source: Together, these data support a conclusion that LGC-46 and ACC-4 function together in cholinergic motor neurons to regulate the SV release kinetics following neuronal activation.
evidence: This is inferred from genetic interaction and electrophysiology data showing both proteins are required for proper regulation of evoked release.

claim: LGC-46 and ACC-4 may form a heteromeric channel.
source: As LGC-46 and ACC-4 both belong to the ACC protein family, it is possible that the proteins may form a heteromeric channel.
evidence: This is speculated based on the family membership and functional interaction.

claim: LGC-46 and ACC-4 may interact indirectly and co-regulate cholinergic release.
source: Alternatively, they may interact indirectly and co-regulate cholinergic release.
evidence: This is presented as an alternative hypothesis to direct heteromeric channel formation.

claim: Upon a burst of ACh release, opening of LGC-46 channels limits further SV release in the sustained late phase.
source: As both loss- and gain- of function lgc-46 mutants specifically affect the decay phase, but not the rise phase, of eEPSC, our data support a model where upon a burst of ACh release, opening of LGC-46 channels limits further SV release in the sustained late phase.
evidence: This model is inferred from the observation that lgc-46 mutations specifically affect the decay phase of evoked release.

claim: LGC-46(gf) exhibits a strong inhibitory effect on synaptic release under elevated neuronal activity.
source: LGC-46(gf) also exhibits a strong inhibitory effect on synaptic release under elevated neuronal activity, suggesting that the mutant channel could have increased sensitivity to ligands, higher channel conductance or prolonged open state, thereby affecting the basal activity of the cholinergic motor neurons.
evidence: This is observed from the reduced frequency of endogenous EPSCs in lgc-46(gf) mutants.

claim: The mutant LGC-46(gf) channel could have increased sensitivity to ligands, higher channel conductance or prolonged open state.
source: LGC-46(gf) also exhibits a strong inhibitory effect on synaptic release under elevated neuronal activity, suggesting that the mutant channel could have increased sensitivity to ligands, higher channel conductance or prolonged open state, thereby affecting the basal activity of the cholinergic motor neurons.
evidence: This is speculated as possible mechanisms for the gain-of-function phenotype.

claim: Rapid feedback inhibition of SV release upon stimulation can contribute to temporal resolution of neural activity within the circuit.
source: Rapid feedback inhibition of SV release upon stimulation can contribute to temporal resolution of neural activity within the circuit.
evidence: This is a general statement about the functional significance of the mechanism.

claim: A tightly regulated sharp decay of evoked EPSCs can ensure transient and adequate release of neurotransmitter to match high-frequency stimuli, possibly without triggering desensitization of postsynaptic receptors.
source: A tightly regulated sharp decay of evoked EPSCs can ensure transient and adequate release of neurotransmitter to match high-frequency stimuli, possibly without triggering desensitization of postsynaptic receptors.
evidence: This is inferred as a functional consequence of the observed mechanism.

claim: Sharpening of synaptic activities by presynaptic LGICs can minimize unwanted cross-talks between synapses and neurons, allowing accurate information encoding in high frequency.
source: Sharpening of synaptic activities by presynaptic LGICs can minimize unwanted cross-talks between synapses and neurons, allowing accurate information encoding in high frequency.
evidence: This is inferred as a functional consequence of the observed mechanism.

claim: This mode of neural control may be particularly suited for synapses with graded potential, such as the case in C. elegans and those in the retina of vertebrates.
source: Such mode of neural control can contribute to the overall circuit performance and may be particularly suited for synapses with graded potential, such as the case in C. elegans and those in the retina of vertebrates.
evidence: This is speculated based on the properties of the mechanism and knowledge of synaptic physiology.

claim: Injection of acetylcholine to Aplysia pleural ganglia caused rapid inhibitory postsynaptic potential in a chloride concentration-dependent manner.
source: Injection of acetylcholine to pleural ganglia caused rapid inhibitory postsynaptic potential in a chloride concentration-dependent manner, suggesting the presence of ACh-gated anion channels (Kehoe, 1972a, 1972b; Kehoe and McIntosh, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kehoe, 1972a, 1972b and Kehoe and McIntosh, 1998.

claim: The identity of ACh-gated anion channels in Aplysia remains unknown.
source: The identity of these channels in Aplysia remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge.

claim: The discovery of C. elegans ACC proteins has provided molecular evidence for ACh-gated chloride channels.
source: The discovery of C. elegans ACC proteins has provided molecular evidence for ACh-gated chloride channels (Putrenko et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Putrenko et al., 2005.

claim: Several ACC channels display differential expression in neurons.
source: Several ACC channels are recently shown to display the differential expression in neurons (Pereira et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pereira et al., 2015.

claim: ACC-2 has been implicated in regulation of reversal behavior, presumably as a postsynaptic receptor.
source: ACC-2 has been implicated in regulation of reversal behavior, presumably as a postsynaptic receptor (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2014.

claim: ACC-4 acts as a functional partner of LGC-46 at the presynaptic release site.
source: Our data support a conclusion that ACC-4 acts as a functional partner of LGC-46 at the presynaptic release site.
evidence: This is inferred from genetic interaction and colocalization data.

claim: Increasing presynaptic inhibition using lgc-46(gf) dampens overexcitation in the acr-2(gf) seizure model.
source: Increasing presynaptic inhibition using lgc-46(gf) dampens overexcitation in the acr-2(gf) seizure model.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the suppression of acr-2(gf) convulsions by lgc-46(gf).

claim: The molecular nature and functional properties of acr-2(gf) show similarities to gain of function mutations in human CHRNB2.
source: The molecular nature and functional properties of acr-2(gf) show similarities to gain of function mutations in human CHRNB2, the β2 subunit of neuronal nicotinic receptors, which have been identified as causal in autosomal dominant nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy (Phillips et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Phillips et al., 2001.

claim: Gain of function mutations in human CHRNB2 have been identified as causal in autosomal dominant nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy.
source: The molecular nature and functional properties of acr-2(gf) show similarities to gain of function mutations in human CHRNB2, the β2 subunit of neuronal nicotinic receptors, which have been identified as causal in autosomal dominant nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy (Phillips et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Phillips et al., 2001.

claim: Mutant CHRNB2 proteins result in hyperactive channels and can alter the local circuit activity.
source: Studies using cell lines and transgenic mouse models show that these mutant CHRNB2 proteins result in hyperactive channels, and can alter the local circuit activity (Manfredi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Manfredi et al., 2009.

claim: The hyper-excitation in acr-2(gf) animals can be suppressed by increasing presynaptic inhibition.
source: Our observations that the hyper-excitation in acr-2(gf) animals can be suppressed by increasing presynaptic inhibition suggest alternative ideas to manage circuit dysfunction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the suppression of acr-2(gf) phenotypes by lgc-46(gf).

claim: Malfunction of presynaptic glycine channel can partially contribute to startle disease (hyperekplexia) in a mouse model.
source: For example, malfunction of presynaptic glycine channel can partially contribute to startle disease (hyperekplexia) in a mouse model (Xiong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xiong et al., 2014.

claim: Ionotropic anion channels should be considered potential targets for modulating neuronal circuit function and in treatments for neurological disorders.
source: These findings suggest ionotropic anion channels should be considered potential targets for modulating neuronal circuit function and in treatments for neurological disorders.
evidence: This is inferred from the findings about presynaptic anion channels and their role in circuit function.
